retired_derivation_rows.claim: The chain model's density is $\phi(x)\phi(y-x)\phi(z-y)$, where $\phi$ is the standard-normal density. Its factors are exactly the parent probability kernels $K_X(dx)=N(0,1)(dx)$, $K_Y(x,dy)=N(x,1)(dy)$, and $K_Z(y,dz)=N(y,1)(dz)$, so the full-joint law factorizes in the topological order $X,Y,Z$. All three vertices are observed and [F8] gives the Markovian SCM condition. Its moments are $\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=3$, and distinct covariances $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)=2$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)=1$. The vector is multivariate normal by step 1.1, and its covariance matrix is positive definite because $(X,Y,Z)$ is an invertible triangular linear transform of $(U_X,U_Y,U_Z)$. The conditional covariance formula gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z\mid Y)=1-\frac{1\cdot2}{2}=0,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y\mid Z)=1-\frac{1\cdot2}{3}=\frac13,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z\mid X)=2-\frac{1\cdot1}{1}=1.$ Together with the nonzero marginal covariances, [F4] shows that the only conditional independence between distinct variables is $X\perp Z\mid Y$. By [F10], the only d-separated vertex pair is also $X,Z$ given $Y$: the adjacent pairs have an active one-edge path, and the $X$–$Z$ path is blocked only by conditioning on $Y$. Any conditional independence between vertex sets would imply the corresponding coordinate independences, so the set-level independence and d-separation models also agree. This verifies faithfulness in [F7].

The collider model's density is $\phi(x)\phi(z)\phi(y-x-z)$. Its factors are exactly the parent probability kernels $K_X(dx)=N(0,1)(dx)$, $K_Z(dz)=N(0,1)(dz)$, and $K_Y(x,z,dy)=N(x+z,1)(dy)$, so the full-joint law factorizes in the topological order $X,Z,Y$. All vertices are observed and [F8] gives the Markovian SCM condition. Its variances are $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=3$, its covariances are $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y)=1$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)=0$. The vector is multivariate normal by step 1.1, and this covariance matrix is positive definite by the invertible triangular map from the exogenous variables. The conditional covariances are $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z\mid Y)=0-\frac{1\cdot1}{3}=-\frac13,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y\mid Z)=1,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z\mid X)=1.$ Therefore [F4] shows that $X\perp Z$ marginally, but there is no conditional independence after conditioning on the third variable and no independence for an adjacent pair. By [F10], this is exactly the collider DAG's d-separation list: the collider path is blocked unconditioned and opened by conditioning on $Y$, while each adjacent pair has an active one-edge path. Any set conditional independence would imply coordinate independences, so [F7] holds at the set level as well.

In the latent model, $\mathbb E(X,Y)=(0,0)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, by independence of $L,U_X,U_Y$. In the direct-edge model, $\mathbb E(X,Y)=(0,0)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=2$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$, and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\tfrac14(2)+\tfrac32=2$. Both vectors are Gaussian by step 1.1 and have the same positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, whose leading principal minors are $2$ and $3$. By [F5], both vector characteristic functions equal $\exp(-t^T\Sigma t/2)$ for every $t\in\mathbb R^2$; the uniqueness clause of [F5] gives equality of the full observed laws.

Fix the labels. Multiplication $x_i\mapsto v_i=y_ix_i$ preserves Lebesgue-null sets. Outside a finite union of proper polynomial zero sets, every set of at most $d$ of the $v_i$ is linearly independent and no $d+1$ of them lie in one affine hyperplane. The latter excludes the determinant-zero conditions for the augmented rows $(v_i^T,1)$; the former excludes the appropriate Gram determinant-zero conditions. Each relevant polynomial is nonzero, as witnessed by coordinate vectors for the linear conditions and affinely independent points for the affine conditions. By [F6] under [A1], each of these proper polynomial zero sets is Lebesgue null, and so is their finite union. This is the only inherited Countable Choice use. All first-stage active points lie in the hyperplane $(w^*)^Tv=1$, so their number is at most $d$. Their column matrix $A$ has full column rank, and the dual representation is uniquely $$\alpha=(A^TA)^{-1}\mathbf1,$$ because $A^Tw^*=\mathbf1$ and $w^*=A\alpha$. Each coordinate of this rational function has a polynomial numerator not identically zero: for orthonormal columns, every coordinate is $1$. After excluding these finitely many additional numerator-zero sets for every possible active subset, every active multiplier is nonzero. Since the KKT multipliers are nonnegative, they are all positive. Thus every first-stage active index has a simultaneously positive dual representation; [F4] gives $M=1$, and the expansion of step 2.1 gives $w_t=w^*\log t+O(1)$. Restricting this null-set conclusion to the open set of strictly separable arrays proves exactly the almost-everywhere clause in the Statement. This is a consequence, not an extra general-position assumption on the all-data result.

The pre-reward history is trivial and $A_1=2$ deterministically. Thus for arm 2 the history-and-arm events are $B=\varnothing$ or $B=\Omega$, while for arm 1 only $B=\varnothing$ is possible. For every Borel $C$, the fixed-law identity for $B=\Omega$ is $\mathbb P(\Omega\cap\{Y_1\in C\})=P_2(C)=\mathbb P(\Omega)P_2(C)$ by step 1.1; it is trivial for $B=\varnothing$. The conditional-mean identity likewise holds: for $B=\Omega$, $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B Y_1]=1/2=\mu_2\mathbb P(B)$, and for $B=\varnothing$ both sides are zero.

At each elimination pivot, searching and swapping rows costs $O(d)$ operations; normalizing one row and eliminating its column from at most $d-1$ rows costs $O(d^2)$. The $d$ pivots therefore cost $O(d^3)$. Each matrix update and multiplication by $b_t$ costs $O(d^2)$; one finite-action score costs $O(d^2)$ and a maximization over $m_t$ actions costs $O(d^2m_t)$. Storing the returned feature and reward costs $O(d)$ per round. Summing over $n$ rounds gives $O(nd^3+d^2\sum_{t\in F}m_t)$ operations, and there is exactly one selector call for each $t\in K$.

For each $m\ge1$, put $g_m=2^{-m}\lfloor2^m g\rfloor$. These are finite-valued Borel simple functions increasing pointwise to $g$. Write $g_m=\sum_r c_{m,r}\mathbf 1_{A_{m,r}}$ for Borel level sets $A_{m,r}$ in the full matrix space. By the kernel identity [F4], for every $H\in\mathcal T$,
$$\int_H\int g_m\,dQ_\omega\,d\mathbb P(\omega)=\int_H g_m(W)\,d\mathbb P.$$
The kernel integrals of $g_m$ are $\mathcal T$-measurable finite sums of kernel evaluations. By [F6], they increase to $k(\omega)=\int g\,dQ_\omega$, and the right-hand integrals increase to $\int_H g(W)\,d\mathbb P$. Applying [F6] on both sides gives the same identity with $g$ in place of $g_m$. Thus $k$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable, bounded, and has the defining integral identities of a conditional-expectation version by [F5]. Step 3.1 gives $k\le\alpha$ almost surely, proving the conditional bound.
